faq_blocks.answer:
A is Assertive, one end of the NERIS Identity from 16Personalities, covering overall self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure; it measures no ability and is not a fifth official MBTI dimension.

To see this end, review two real judgements: one backed by data, one only by inference. Compare how confident you were and how much confidence was lost after the rebuttal. That is one observation and cannot decide the suffix — either end may change the plan the moment it is contradicted.

faq_blocks.answer:
No. The four letters come from the MBTI preference system, and A comes from the NERIS description used by 16Personalities; the same code does not mean the scales, items or scores can be exchanged.

NERIS borrows the four-letter notation and adds the Identity suffix inside its own system. The four letters cover the direction of attention, the material, the standard of judgement and the outer arrangement, not only how information is taken in and settled; the suffix describes how you assess your own judgement. When reading a report, check the instrument name and item version first, then read the four-letter explanation and the Identity explanation separately, and never add or convert the scores from the two.

faq_blocks.answer:
No. The Assertive suffix describes self-assurance and reactions to stress in NERIS. To assess a decision, look at the evidence, the options considered and the trade-offs.

Someone can feel sure about a draft and still spend more time checking an external delivery commitment. How quickly to decide depends in part on what it would cost to reverse the decision.

faq_blocks.answer:
There is no such conversion. Ne and Ti are theoretical concepts in type dynamics; a NERIS A/T result cannot be used to infer the strength of these functions.

Ne and Ti describe how possibility is found outside and consistency checked inside, and how well that is done depends on training and setting. Two people may both love taking a problem apart, one advancing through live conversation and the other through private reasoning. The two systems have their own items and scoring, and reading one result as a function score in the other has no basis.

faq_blocks.answer:
No. Being less unsettled by pressure is not the same as refusing feedback, and it does not guarantee that feedback was understood.

You can repeat the other person's words back and ask whether that is what they meant. If the words were "this estimate is too optimistic" and you heard "the whole plan is unusable", you are not discussing the same thing. After restating, ask which condition would change your mind.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Read the four letters and the suffix separately. ENTP is a four-letter type code. The -A identifies the Assertive end of 16Personalities’ separate Identity scale.

Extraversion and Introversion describe where attention and energy tend to go. Intuition and Sensing describe whether someone tends to notice patterns and possibilities or concrete details and experience. Thinking and Feeling describe how someone weighs impersonal criteria or human values and circumstances when making decisions. Judging and Perceiving describe whether someone prefers more structure or more room to adjust in the outside world.

The ENTP function stack used here is dominant extraverted Intuition (Ne), auxiliary introverted Thinking (Ti), tertiary Feeling written as Fe, and inferior introverted Sensing (Si). The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists Fe or Fi for tertiary Feeling. These positions describe type dynamics and do not tell you how a person will act or perform.

The third letter, T, stands for Thinking and concerns the criteria someone tends to use in a decision. The -A after the hyphen stands for Assertive and concerns self-assurance. If a report shows ENTP-T instead, the -T stands for Turbulent. Check the assessment provider before interpreting either result.

Assertive and Turbulent describe how people evaluate themselves under pressure. Confidence cannot correct a faulty premise. A person who usually double-checks may be satisfied after a single review if the evidence is clear.

Two reports may carry different suffixes. If one sitting brings to mind a choice with data and the other a review that could only proceed on assumptions, record what each was referring to, then check the instrument and the item version. Recent experience may shape which situation you recall while answering, but inferring why a score moved from that is not sound.

### How ENTP-A and ENTP-T differ

The two differ at the Identity end: under the same pressure and the same rebuttal, whether your confidence in your own judgement changes. The A end is generally described as more confident and less unsettled by pressure; the T end doubts itself more and is more sensitive to stress. That does not mean more rigorous reasoning, and it does not mean one of them cannot hear opposition.

Nor does it decide who proposes and who reviews. Either end can check constraints and look for counterexamples on the same material; checking the cost table, asking someone to review the argument and rewriting the premises are used at both ends and say nothing about which end someone is on. Writing "who proposes and who checks" into a division of work should rest on information, responsibility and deadline, not on a suffix.
sections.title: ENTP-A letters and framework

sections.body_md:
When one rebuttal lands, three things can be separated: whether your confidence in the original judgement dropped, whether you subjectively felt rejected, and what you actually did next. The three do not always move together.

In a fictional technical review, the same three options, estimates, budget and deadline are on the table. A colleague says the proposal will not hold up in six months and offers no new data. Two people might both ask whether the concern is the cost estimate or the expected growth. After checking the same evidence, one might still trust most of the recommendation, while the other might feel less sure about their judgment. Either could revise the recommendation if the evidence warrants it. Confidence and the decision to revise are separate observations.

Agreeing on the specific claim to check can move the discussion forward. If it turns out that the estimate leaves out maintenance costs, revise the estimate regardless of how confident anyone felt.

| Under this condition | What can be done | The cost to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Just taking on an unfamiliar field | Push a first version with the existing frame and fill in material as it runs | Ask first whether there are industry conventions you do not yet know |
| The plan is rejected in public | Separate whether the premise or the conclusion was moved | Repeat the other person's words back, so you do not answer the wrong question |
| The discussion goes in circles | Name one point of disagreement that can be verified, and agree how a result is counted | State the cost of verifying up front; do not let the other person pay it |
| A colleague disagrees | Offer a small version that can be tried, with scope and time fixed | Someone has to look at the result afterwards, or it is only another start |
| The same task for three months | Look for a counterexample on purpose at intervals | Find a real counterexample, not an easy win |
| Ten minutes left in the review | Ask which premise is most likely to be overturned | Under time pressure, "nobody objected" easily becomes "checked" |

These rows are general practice available at either end; they describe task conditions and costs, not evidence for one end.
sections.title: ENTP-A core patterns, value and counterexamples

sections.body_md:
Before settling on an option at work, ask who bears the cost if it is wrong, when that cost will become clear and how easily you can reverse the decision. The suffix does not answer any of those questions.

For something that only affects your own next draft, doing first and changing later usually saves time; for something that affects other people's schedules, budget or external commitments, the premises are worth laying out first. Saying "I'll write it this way and can change it by tomorrow night" in a group chat costs little; setting next quarter's direction for the team costs a great deal to reverse. The same person moves at different speeds in these two situations, and that says nothing about the suffix.

If a colleague says, “You’re oversimplifying this,” ask what the proposal missed. An underestimated workload calls for a better estimate. Uncertainty about whether people will use it calls for feedback from those affected.

### ENTP-A at work or study: make the first step small

With thin information, some people give the conclusion first and add material later; designing the first step to be reversible and to bring back new information is more practical than suppressing the habit.

In a fictional mentoring exercise, ask a new colleague to write a one-page comparison using shared criteria. Review the draft together and discuss any criterion they missed or interpreted differently.

In a fictional example, send your three main points to two people attending your presentation. Ask which point needs stronger evidence and use the answers to choose where to start. Label claims that are still provisional. Afterwards, ask what was unclear and where people disagreed. If the same point causes confusion in the next session, revise that slide.
sections.title: ENTP-A work and career exploration

sections.body_md:
What can be discussed in a relationship is commitment, listening, frequency and boundaries, not an impression such as who is more confident.

In a fictional conversation, a partner says, “You never let me finish.” Before listing counterexamples, ask which moment they mean. You might say, “Are you thinking of last week, when I jumped in before you had finished?” That gives both people an event they can discuss.

Jokes work the same way. A tease you find harmless may stay with the other person for a long time. Adding one real opinion after the joke lands works better than explaining afterwards that no harm was meant.

### ENTP-A: turning a win into agreement

After you explain your position, give the other person room to disagree and identify what is open to revision.

State your conclusion, explain what evidence supports it and say which part you are willing to reconsider. If someone challenges that part, ask what they see differently before deciding what to keep.

Frequency is worth agreeing too: one person wants a daily check-in, the other thinks once a week is enough. The difference itself is not the problem; saying it clearly keeps "no reply" from being read as "no interest".
sections.title: ENTP-A relationships and communication

sections.body_md:
It is possible to keep confidence in the direction while checking whether you are already overloaded. Under high pressure, some people carry the meeting on improvisation and prepare less — a common reaction, not a direct result of the suffix, and not proof that this end copes better.

It saves effort in the short term and may push rework onto other people later. External signals are more reliable than self-perception: the same item reworked twice, starting to change other people's files without confirming, a meeting that ends with nobody remembering the conclusion. When these appear, decide which commitment to reduce first by its effect on delivery, without waiting for a full set.

Moving into an unfamiliar field, confidence in your own judgement may drop a notch. How a new industry defines good work, who holds a veto, which traps are not written down — none of it is clear yet, and asking more questions is a reasonable cost. Once those are filled in, the pace usually returns. Rather than blaming yourself for "becoming cautious", split it three ways: not enough information, unclear authority, relationships not yet established.

With persistent insomnia, prolonged low mood, or clear effects on daily work, seek professional support early rather than absorbing it alone.
sections.title: ENTP-A stress and recovery

sections.body_md:
For a reflection exercise, choose a proposal and write down three assumptions about cost, demand or maintenance. For each one, note what would change your mind. Record what the evidence shows and how you felt about your judgment before and after checking. The exercise can reveal how you respond to feedback. It cannot establish an A/T suffix.

Set the verification deadline by the premise's impact, not by a fixed number of days: for anything affecting budget and external delivery, name one piece of evidence that must arrive before the decision; for something affecting only the next draft, fill it in as you go. An observation window also works, such as until the next review; if the key evidence has not arrived by then, take the assumption into the meeting but do not make an irreversible commitment on it. That is closer to the real risk than deciding whether a meeting can happen by counting items.

Record counterexamples too: sometimes a premise you defended turned out wrong, and sometimes one you dropped actually held. Writing both down is more useful than recording only successes. Check the constraints beyond your own proposal as well — whether another approach is cheaper under the same budget and delivery date deserves a row too.

Decide before you start what evidence would be enough to act. If you reach that threshold, document what remains uncertain and who will revisit it if new evidence comes in. The number of checks alone says little about the quality of the decision or your suffix.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The suffix follows the [16Personalities explanation of NERIS](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory), and the original definition of Identity is in the [framework's article on Assertive and Turbulent](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent); the four letters follow the public description of the MBTI preference system. This page borrows the NERIS Identity concept to explain the suffix and does not thereby claim that FermatMind and NERIS use the same items, scoring or norms; the scope of this site's implementation is limited to what the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence) set out.

**The four-position convention used here.** The function stack follows the common four-function notation used on this page, with ENTP as dominant Ne, auxiliary Ti, third Fe and fourth Si. Position describes emphasis in preference, not a task order or a level of ability; the attitude of the third process, Fe, differs between authors and is not treated here as any institution's only account. Position is not used to infer a field of competence, career fit or relationship outcome.

**Fictional examples.** The technical review, mentoring exercise, presentation, relationship conversation, workload examples and proposal exercise illustrate ways to respond to feedback. They do not describe real people or establish a suffix.

**Scope limits.** The four letters and the suffix belong to different layers, and codes of the same shape cannot be converted. The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate the number of people at either NERIS A/T end. This page is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; anything involving medicine, first aid, electricity or driving is treated here only as communication and information sorting, and the actual handling should be taken to professional help first under professional guidance, with clinical judgement left to a qualified professional.

profile.excerpt: The A in ENTP-A comes from the NERIS framework used by 16Personalities, Assertive in English. It describes the layer of self-assessment: how confident you are in the reasoning you have just run, and whether that confidence holds when pressure arrives. The A end is generally described as more confident in its own judgement and less unsettled by pressure; that does not mean the reasoning is tighter.
profile.title: What Does ENTP-A Mean? The Assertive Suffix Explained

sections.body_md:
In ENTP-A, the -A stands for Assertive on 16Personalities’ NERIS Identity scale. The scale describes self-assurance and reactions to stress. Someone closer to the Assertive end may feel more confident after being challenged. The suffix adds no official MBTI preference and tells you nothing about how well someone argues or decides.

ENTP stands for Extraversion, Intuition, Thinking and Perceiving. Those four MBTI preferences concern attention and energy, information, decision criteria and how someone approaches the outside world. The NERIS suffix belongs to a separate measure. Even after reviewing the same evidence, two people may feel differently about their original judgment.

| Core profile | How to read ENTP-A |
| --- | --- |
| Four letters | Extraversion (E), Intuition (N), Thinking (T) and Perceiving (P) |
| What the suffix means | A is Assertive, the self-assured end |
| Which framework | The NERIS Identity used by 16Personalities; not a fifth official MBTI dimension |
| What it describes | Overall self-assessment, self-assurance, subjective response to pressure |
| What it does not describe | Ability, debate skills, decision quality or career fit |
| Difference from ENTP-T | After the same pressure and checks, someone closer to Assertive may stay confident, while someone closer to Turbulent may feel more doubt. |

The table compares how people may feel about their judgment after the same challenge. Either person can check the evidence immediately or put the proposal aside. One instance of feedback cannot establish a suffix.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Read the four letters and the suffix separately. ENTP is a four-letter type code. The -A identifies the Assertive end of 16Personalities’ separate Identity scale.

Extraversion and Introversion describe where attention and energy tend to go. Intuition and Sensing describe whether someone tends to notice patterns and possibilities or concrete details and experience. Thinking and Feeling describe how someone weighs impersonal criteria or human values and circumstances when making decisions. Judging and Perceiving describe whether someone prefers more structure or more room to adjust in the outside world.

The ENTP function stack used here is dominant extraverted Intuition (Ne), auxiliary introverted Thinking (Ti), tertiary Feeling written as Fe, and inferior introverted Sensing (Si). The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists Fe or Fi for tertiary Feeling. These positions describe type dynamics and do not tell you how a person will act or perform.

The third letter, T, stands for Thinking and concerns the criteria someone tends to use in a decision. The -A after the hyphen stands for Assertive and concerns self-assurance. If a report shows ENTP-T instead, the -T stands for Turbulent. Check the assessment provider before interpreting either result.

Assertive and Turbulent describe how people evaluate themselves under pressure. Confidence cannot correct a faulty premise. A person who usually double-checks may be satisfied after a single review if the evidence is clear.

Two reports may carry different suffixes. If one sitting brings to mind a choice with data and the other a review that could only proceed on assumptions, record what each was referring to, then check the instrument and the item version. Recent experience may shape which situation you recall while answering, but inferring why a score moved from that is not sound.

### How ENTP-A and ENTP-T differ

The two differ at the Identity end: under the same pressure and the same rebuttal, whether your confidence in your own judgement changes. The A end is generally described as more confident and less unsettled by pressure; the T end doubts itself more and is more sensitive to stress. That does not mean more rigorous reasoning, and it does not mean one of them cannot hear opposition.

Nor does it decide who proposes and who reviews. Either end can check constraints and look for counterexamples on the same material; checking the cost table, asking someone to review the argument and rewriting the premises are used at both ends and say nothing about which end someone is on. Writing "who proposes and who checks" into a division of work should rest on information, responsibility and deadline, not on a suffix.
sections.title: ENTP-A letters and framework

sections.body_md:
When one rebuttal lands, three things can be separated: whether your confidence in the original judgement dropped, whether you subjectively felt rejected, and what you actually did next. The three do not always move together.

In a fictional technical review, the same three options, estimates, budget and deadline are on the table. A colleague says the proposal will not hold up in six months and offers no new data. Two people might both ask whether the concern is the cost estimate or the expected growth. After checking the same evidence, one might still trust most of the recommendation, while the other might feel less sure about their judgment. Either could revise the recommendation if the evidence warrants it. Confidence and the decision to revise are separate observations.

Agreeing on the specific claim to check can move the discussion forward. If it turns out that the estimate leaves out maintenance costs, revise the estimate regardless of how confident anyone felt.

| Under this condition | What can be done | The cost to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Just taking on an unfamiliar field | Push a first version with the existing frame and fill in material as it runs | Ask first whether there are industry conventions you do not yet know |
| The plan is rejected in public | Separate whether the premise or the conclusion was moved | Repeat the other person's words back, so you do not answer the wrong question |
| The discussion goes in circles | Name one point of disagreement that can be verified, and agree how a result is counted | State the cost of verifying up front; do not let the other person pay it |
| A colleague disagrees | Offer a small version that can be tried, with scope and time fixed | Someone has to look at the result afterwards, or it is only another start |
| The same task for three months | Look for a counterexample on purpose at intervals | Find a real counterexample, not an easy win |
| Ten minutes left in the review | Ask which premise is most likely to be overturned | Under time pressure, "nobody objected" easily becomes "checked" |

These rows are general practice available at either end; they describe task conditions and costs, not evidence for one end.
sections.title: ENTP-A core patterns, value and counterexamples

sections.body_md:
Before settling on an option at work, ask who bears the cost if it is wrong, when that cost will become clear and how easily you can reverse the decision. The suffix does not answer any of those questions.

For something that only affects your own next draft, doing first and changing later usually saves time; for something that affects other people's schedules, budget or external commitments, the premises are worth laying out first. Saying "I'll write it this way and can change it by tomorrow night" in a group chat costs little; setting next quarter's direction for the team costs a great deal to reverse. The same person moves at different speeds in these two situations, and that says nothing about the suffix.

If a colleague says, “You’re oversimplifying this,” ask what the proposal missed. An underestimated workload calls for a better estimate. Uncertainty about whether people will use it calls for feedback from those affected.

### ENTP-A at work or study: make the first step small

With thin information, some people give the conclusion first and add material later; designing the first step to be reversible and to bring back new information is more practical than suppressing the habit.

In a fictional mentoring exercise, ask a new colleague to write a one-page comparison using shared criteria. Review the draft together and discuss any criterion they missed or interpreted differently.

In a fictional example, send your three main points to two people attending your presentation. Ask which point needs stronger evidence and use the answers to choose where to start. Label claims that are still provisional. Afterwards, ask what was unclear and where people disagreed. If the same point causes confusion in the next session, revise that slide.
sections.title: ENTP-A work and career exploration

sections.body_md:
What can be discussed in a relationship is commitment, listening, frequency and boundaries, not an impression such as who is more confident.

In a fictional conversation, a partner says, “You never let me finish.” Before listing counterexamples, ask which moment they mean. You might say, “Are you thinking of last week, when I jumped in before you had finished?” That gives both people an event they can discuss.

Jokes work the same way. A tease you find harmless may stay with the other person for a long time. Adding one real opinion after the joke lands works better than explaining afterwards that no harm was meant.

### ENTP-A: turning a win into agreement

After you explain your position, give the other person room to disagree and identify what is open to revision.

State your conclusion, explain what evidence supports it and say which part you are willing to reconsider. If someone challenges that part, ask what they see differently before deciding what to keep.

Frequency is worth agreeing too: one person wants a daily check-in, the other thinks once a week is enough. The difference itself is not the problem; saying it clearly keeps "no reply" from being read as "no interest".
sections.title: ENTP-A relationships and communication

sections.body_md:
It is possible to keep confidence in the direction while checking whether you are already overloaded. Under high pressure, some people carry the meeting on improvisation and prepare less — a common reaction, not a direct result of the suffix, and not proof that this end copes better.

It saves effort in the short term and may push rework onto other people later. External signals are more reliable than self-perception: the same item reworked twice, starting to change other people's files without confirming, a meeting that ends with nobody remembering the conclusion. When these appear, decide which commitment to reduce first by its effect on delivery, without waiting for a full set.

Moving into an unfamiliar field, confidence in your own judgement may drop a notch. How a new industry defines good work, who holds a veto, which traps are not written down — none of it is clear yet, and asking more questions is a reasonable cost. Once those are filled in, the pace usually returns. Rather than blaming yourself for "becoming cautious", split it three ways: not enough information, unclear authority, relationships not yet established.

With persistent insomnia, prolonged low mood, or clear effects on daily work, seek professional support early rather than absorbing it alone.
sections.title: ENTP-A stress and recovery

sections.body_md:
For a reflection exercise, choose a proposal and write down three assumptions about cost, demand or maintenance. For each one, note what would change your mind. Record what the evidence shows and how you felt about your judgment before and after checking. The exercise can reveal how you respond to feedback. It cannot establish an A/T suffix.

Set the verification deadline by the premise's impact, not by a fixed number of days: for anything affecting budget and external delivery, name one piece of evidence that must arrive before the decision; for something affecting only the next draft, fill it in as you go. An observation window also works, such as until the next review; if the key evidence has not arrived by then, take the assumption into the meeting but do not make an irreversible commitment on it. That is closer to the real risk than deciding whether a meeting can happen by counting items.

Record counterexamples too: sometimes a premise you defended turned out wrong, and sometimes one you dropped actually held. Writing both down is more useful than recording only successes. Check the constraints beyond your own proposal as well — whether another approach is cheaper under the same budget and delivery date deserves a row too.

Decide before you start what evidence would be enough to act. If you reach that threshold, document what remains uncertain and who will revisit it if new evidence comes in. The number of checks alone says little about the quality of the decision or your suffix.

- [ENTP-T: self-doubt and the pressure scenes compared](/en/personality/entp-t)

These pages differ in which letters are shared and which positions differ: the ENTP profile shares all four letters and differs only in whether a suffix is attached; ENTP-T shares the same four letters and differs at one end of Identity; ENFP shares E, N and P, with a different basis of judgement in T and F. Bring one concrete example of your own when reading; it is more useful than memorising conclusions.
sections.title: ENTP-A related types and comparisons

items.answer:
A is Assertive, one end of the NERIS Identity from 16Personalities, covering overall self-assessment, self-assurance and response to pressure; it measures no ability and is not a fifth official MBTI dimension.

To see this end, review two real judgements: one backed by data, one only by inference. Compare how confident you were and how much confidence was lost after the rebuttal. That is one observation and cannot decide the suffix — either end may change the plan the moment it is contradicted.
items.question: What does the A in ENTP-A mean?

items.answer:
No. The four letters come from the MBTI preference system, and A comes from the NERIS description used by 16Personalities; the same code does not mean the scales, items or scores can be exchanged.

NERIS borrows the four-letter notation and adds the Identity suffix inside its own system. The four letters cover the direction of attention, the material, the standard of judgement and the outer arrangement, not only how information is taken in and settled; the suffix describes how you assess your own judgement. When reading a report, check the instrument name and item version first, then read the four-letter explanation and the Identity explanation separately, and never add or convert the scores from the two.
items.question: Are ENTP-A and the four letters the same system?

items.answer:
No. The Assertive suffix describes self-assurance and reactions to stress in NERIS. To assess a decision, look at the evidence, the options considered and the trade-offs.

Someone can feel sure about a draft and still spend more time checking an external delivery commitment. How quickly to decide depends in part on what it would cost to reverse the decision.
items.question: Does ENTP-A Tell You Who Will Make Better Decisions?

items.answer:
There is no such conversion. Ne and Ti are theoretical concepts in type dynamics; a NERIS A/T result cannot be used to infer the strength of these functions.

Ne and Ti describe how possibility is found outside and consistency checked inside, and how well that is done depends on training and setting. Two people may both love taking a problem apart, one advancing through live conversation and the other through private reasoning. The two systems have their own items and scoring, and reading one result as a function score in the other has no basis.
items.question: Are Ne or Ti stronger in ENTP-A?

items.answer:
No. Ask the other person to name the specific constraint, evidence or risk threshold first, then decide what to check; the three have no fixed order and two may need changing at once.

When someone says the approach will not hold up, ask them to point to the specific place, then turn the argument into a checkable question: what were the maintenance hours for similar projects after six months, and what proportion of the last architecture change was reworked? If such figures are to be used, first confirm that scale, period and definitions are comparable, and state which part of the judgement they can support — usable for a decision when comparable, only indicative when not.
items.question: ENTP-A: when people object to my plan, should I accept all of it?

items.answer:
No. Being less unsettled by pressure is not the same as refusing feedback, and it does not guarantee that feedback was understood.

You can repeat the other person's words back and ask whether that is what they meant. If the words were "this estimate is too optimistic" and you heard "the whole plan is unusable", you are not discussing the same thing. After restating, ask which condition would change your mind.
items.question: ENTP-A: if I am not much affected, does that mean I do not listen?

items.answer:
Yes. Both ends doubt: you may still hesitate after giving a conclusion, look for someone to verify it, and overturn a settled direction; those actions say more about what you lack at that moment than about the suffix.

Recent experience may shape which situation you recall while answering, but it cannot establish why a score moved. If you compare two results, first confirm the same instrument and item version, then record what each was referring to; one retest does not prove which was more accurate. When support is needed, describing the specific point where you are stuck to an appropriate person is more direct than testing again.
items.question: Can ENTP-A also doubt itself and want help?

items.answer:
It depends on what you are missing: the four letters, the detail of the other end, or how the two compare.

The overall framework of the four letters is on the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp); for the T end, go to [ENTP-T](/en/personality/entp-t); the two are set side by side on the [same-type comparison](/en/personality/entp-a-vs-entp-t). Bring one real example when reading; it is more useful than memorising conclusions.
items.question: What Should I Read Next About ENTP-A?

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The suffix follows the [16Personalities explanation of NERIS](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory), and the original definition of Identity is in the [framework's article on Assertive and Turbulent](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent); the four letters follow the public description of the MBTI preference system. This page borrows the NERIS Identity concept to explain the suffix and does not thereby claim that FermatMind and NERIS use the same items, scoring or norms; the scope of this site's implementation is limited to what the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence) set out.

**The four-position convention used here.** The function stack follows the common four-function notation used on this page, with ENTP as dominant Ne, auxiliary Ti, third Fe and fourth Si. Position describes emphasis in preference, not a task order or a level of ability; the attitude of the third process, Fe, differs between authors and is not treated here as any institution's only account. Position is not used to infer a field of competence, career fit or relationship outcome.

**Fictional examples.** The technical review, mentoring exercise, presentation, relationship conversation, workload examples and proposal exercise illustrate ways to respond to feedback. They do not describe real people or establish a suffix.

**Scope limits.** The four letters and the suffix belong to different layers, and codes of the same shape cannot be converted. The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate the number of people at either NERIS A/T end. This page is not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; anything involving medicine, first aid, electricity or driving is treated here only as communication and information sorting, and the actual handling should be taken to professional help first under professional guidance, with clinical judgement left to a qualified professional.
